introduction-the-it-works-on-my-machine-.core: Metrics say CPU is at 90%, and traces say a span took 2 s, but neither says which function burned the CPU or allocated the memory. Profilers answer that, but traditionally only locally, briefly and on demand, so production-only issues (real data, real concurrency) are missed. Continuous profiling samples stack traces in production all the time at low overhead, so you can see code-level hotspots for any service at any time.

first_principles.problem: A service uses twice the CPU in production as in staging, and nobody can reproduce it locally.

analogy.title: A fitness tracker vs a one-off doctor visit
analogy.story: A tracker records all day, catching what a brief check-up never sees.
analogy.breaks: Trackers measure one person; profilers aggregate across a fleet.

example.title: Production-only hotspot
flow: Only triggered by real payload shapes

check.q: What question does profiling answer that metrics and traces don't?
check.a: Which functions or lines of code are consuming CPU or memory.

how-it-works-sampling-and-stack-traces.core: Sampling profilers interrupt a process at a fixed rate (say 100 times per second), record the current call stack, and count how often each stack appears. Functions present in many samples are where time is spent. Stacks are symbolised (addresses to function names) and aggregated into profiles per interval. Low rates keep overhead small but statistically accurate over time, and different profile types sample different events (CPU time, allocations, locks).

first_principles.problem: Instrumenting every function call to measure time slows the service by 10× and skews results.

analogy.title: Photographing an office every few seconds
analogy.story: Count how often people are seen in each room to know where time is spent, without timing every movement.
analogy.breaks: Photos might miss brief visits; rare short functions can be under-sampled.

code.text:
curl -s 'http://svc:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30' > cpu.pb.gz
go tool pprof -top cpu.pb.gz | head
#  flat  flat%   cum   cum%
#  4.2s  35.0%  4.5s  37.5%  regexp.(*Regexp).doExecute

check.q: Why are sampling profilers suitable for production while instrumenting profilers often aren't?
check.a: Sampling has small, bounded overhead; instrumenting every call adds large overhead and distorts timings.

the-visualization-flamegraphs.core: A flamegraph stacks call frames vertically, with the root at the bottom and callees above. Each box's width is proportional to the number of samples containing that frame, meaning time spent in it and its children. The x-axis is not time; it's sorted alphabetically to merge identical stacks. Look for wide plateaus at the top (self time) and wide towers to find hotspots, and use diff flamegraphs to compare versions.

first_principles.problem: Engineers stare at a flamegraph thinking left-to-right is a timeline and draw wrong conclusions.

analogy.title: A city skyline where width is floor area
analogy.story: Wide buildings hold the most people (time); tall buildings are just deep call chains.
analogy.breaks: Skylines are geographic; flamegraph order is alphabetical.

example.title: Reading one
flow: json.Marshal() wide flat top = self time

check.q: What does the horizontal axis of a flamegraph represent?
check.a: Not time; frames are sorted (usually alphabetically) so identical stacks merge, and width shows share of samples.

memory-profiling-its-not-just-cpu.core: Memory profiles answer different questions. Allocation profiles show which code allocates the most bytes or objects (driving GC pressure and CPU); in-use or heap profiles show what currently holds memory (leaks, bloat); and goroutine, thread or lock profiles show blocking. In GC'd languages, reducing allocations often cuts CPU and latency more than optimising compute. Compare heap profiles over time to find leaks.

first_principles.problem: A Java service's p99 latency spikes during GC pauses, but CPU profiles show nothing obvious.

analogy.title: Tracking shopping vs what's in the cupboard
analogy.story: Receipts show what you buy (allocations); the cupboard shows what you keep (heap). A cupboard that keeps filling means you never throw anything out.
analogy.breaks: Cupboards are visible; heaps need profiles to inspect.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Leak located in an unbounded cache.

code.text:
curl -s http://svc:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap1.pb.gz
sleep 3600
curl -s http://svc:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap2.pb.gz
go tool pprof -base heap1.pb.gz -sample_index=inuse_space -top heap2.pb.gz | head
# growth concentrated in cache.(*LRU).Add → unbounded map

check.q: What's the difference between allocation and in-use heap profiles?
check.a: Allocation profiles show total memory allocated over time (GC pressure); in-use profiles show memory currently retained (leaks/bloat).

the-tools-pyroscope-and-parca.core: Grafana Pyroscope stores and queries continuous profiles from language SDKs (Go, Java, Python, Ruby, .NET, Node) and from eBPF agents via Grafana Alloy, with flamegraph and diff UIs and labels for slicing by service, version or pod. Parca is an open-source, eBPF-first profiler (Parca Agent) with symbolisation, storage and pprof compatibility. Both use labels like metrics and support comparing time ranges.

first_principles.problem: The team needs fleet-wide always-on profiling without adding SDKs to every legacy service.
derivation: Use **eBPF agents** for broad CPU coverage.
Use **SDKs** for alloc/lock profiles and app labels.

analogy.title: A city-wide CCTV system with searchable tags
analogy.story: Cameras everywhere (eBPF) plus detailed cameras in key buildings (SDKs), all searchable by location and time.
analogy.breaks: CCTV records video; profilers aggregate statistics.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: CPU, memory and lock profiles labelled by version.

check.q: What do language SDK profilers offer that eBPF CPU profilers often don't?
check.a: Allocation, heap and lock profiles with language-level detail and custom application labels.

connecting-profiling-to-the-rest-of-your.core: Profiles become far more useful when linked to other signals. Metrics show a CPU spike, so jump to profiles for that service and time. A trace shows a slow span, so span profiles (profiles tagged with span or trace IDs) show which code ran during it. Deploy annotations tell you to compare profiles before and after the release. Shared labels such as service, version and pod make those jumps seamless.

first_principles.problem: Engineers see a slow span in a trace but can't tell what code made it slow without manual profiling.
truths: Each signal answers a different question.

analogy.title: A detective's case board
analogy.story: Strings connect the CCTV (metrics), witness statements (traces) and forensic lab report (profiles) for the same event.
analogy.breaks: Detectives connect clues manually; tools do it via labels.
